title: Your Pickup Timestamp Is Now a Duty Document: Running Canada–U.S. Lanes on Tariff Deadlines
summary: Canada's Sept 8 surtax and U.S. Section 338 duties turned carrier timestamps into duty evidence. How cross-border fleets and brokers should adapt.
body_markdown:
On September 7, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) published Customs Notice 26-23. Paragraph 19 deserves a spot above every cross-border dispatch board. U.S. goods that were "in transit to Canada" when the new surtax took effect on September 8 were exempt, but only if the importer could prove the goods were bound for Canada and "under the control of a carrier." The proof the notice lists is a bill of lading, report of entry documents, and cargo control documents.


Read that again with a 25% or 50% surtax on value for duty in mind. On a high-value load, whether your customer paid or didn't could come down to whether your pickup time, your cargo control number, and your trip record agree with each other. That is a carrier and broker data problem, not just a customs broker problem. And with Canada–U.S. trade now moving on policy deadlines instead of seasons, September 8 will not be the last cutover.


## What changed between July and September


The sequence matters because each date reset demand on a different side of the border.


-


**July 1, 2026.** The United States declined to extend CUSMA at the joint review. The agreement remains in force, but it now runs on annual reviews instead of a fresh 16-year term.


-


**July 20.** Three U.S. proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 imposed an additional 50% duty on specified Canadian goods. The lists cover alcohol, dairy, and a broad motor-vehicle annex that reaches into food, furniture, machinery, and other products. CUSMA qualification does not exempt covered goods, and Section 338 duties have no built-in expiry.


-


**August 22.** After a three-day suspension, the U.S. duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern, keyed to goods entered for consumption on or after that minute.


-


**September 8.** Canada's United States Surtax Order (2026) applied 15%, 25%, or 50% surtaxes to a matched list of U.S.-origin goods. Importers declare them on the CARM commercial accounting declaration using dedicated surtax codes.


Every truck carrying a date-sensitive load spent those weeks racing a clock it did not set.


## The imbalance keeps changing direction


Statistics Canada's August trade release (October 6) shows the first wave clearly. Exports to the United States rose 8.1% in the month, imports from the U.S. fell 2.5%, and Canada's surplus with the U.S. jumped from $6.1 billion to $11.2 billion, the largest positive monthly change since 1997. A big part of that was U.S. buyers pulling Canadian product south ahead of August 22.


Then the flow reversed. Ahead of September 8, shippers frontloaded northbound, and trade press reported northbound spot rates spiking while southbound volumes in lumber, auto, and steel stayed soft. By late September, market updates were describing southbound freight outperforming northbound again, with capacity tighter on many Canada-to-U.S. lanes and that imbalance expected to run through October.


Underneath the swings, the base is thin. U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics border data shows 439,429 trucks entering the U.S. from Canada in July 2026, down 2.4% year over year, after a 17.0% drop in January. Trade press noted that July cross-border truck freight value hit a record while total weight slipped about 1%. A Canadian load-board truck index has capacity near a five-year low, and a monthly cross-border difficulty index read 58 for the Canada corridor in September, where anything above 50 means harder than the historical norm.


The practical takeaway: a Canada–U.S. lane is not one lane. It is two directional markets, and the headhaul can swap sides on a proclamation date.


## Failure mode one: the timestamp nobody trusted


In most shops, the "loaded" or "departed" time on a cross-border shipment has several authors. The driver taps a status in an app. A dispatcher closes it out later. The shipper prints a bill of lading date. The ACI eManifest trip goes out when someone gets to it. The cargo control number on the paperwork may or may not match the one on the trip.


For 50 weeks a year, nobody looks closely. During a surtax cutover, an importer asks for proof that the goods were under carrier control before the effective date, and your records become the evidence. If your system says the load departed at 06:40 on September 8 because a dispatcher back-filled statuses the next morning, your record now contradicts the driver's log and the shipper's paper. That costs your customer real money and can cost you the account.


CBSA's carrier memorandum (D3-1-1) already requires every carrier to use its own CBSA carrier code on cargo control documents. The decision for leaders is whether pickup and departure are captured as source events (time, location, who recorded it) or as editable fields. If edits are allowed, they should leave an audit trail with a reason. For brokers, the cargo control number and actual pickup time should come back from the carrier at pickup, not at invoicing.


## Failure mode two: quotes that outlive the policy they were priced under


When directional demand reprices within days of a policy announcement, a 30-day cross-border quote is a free option you sold the shipper. A northbound rate quoted in early August could easily be underwater by early September for anyone repositioning empties to cover it.


Leaders have a few levers, and the right mix depends on the book:


-


**Shorter validity on Canada–U.S. quotes** than on domestic, with an explicit expiry rather than "until revised."


-


**A policy-event reopener** in contract freight that triggers on a defined tariff or surtax effective date affecting the commodity or the lane.


-


**Directional rate tables** that let northbound and southbound float separately, rather than one round-trip number that hides which side is subsidizing the other.


Asset carriers with dedicated southbound lumber or auto programs have the most exposure here. When that freight goes soft, the northbound leg stops being a backhaul and becomes the headhaul, and their pricing has to say so.


## Failure mode three: border dwell you can't bill


The new surtax adds more ways for a release to stall. Since May 20, 2025, importers that want release prior to payment must post their own financial security in the CARM Client Portal, and a customs broker can't account for goods until the importer has delegated authority there. Add new surtax codes, origin questions, and HS classification checks on covered goods, and any gap on the importer side can leave the truck parked at the line.


Most rate cons handle detention at the shipper and receiver well and border dwell badly. Define when the border clock starts (arrival at the port, or the ACI arrival record), how long the free time runs, and who pays when release is held for importer-side reasons the carrier can't control. Then make sure your system records port arrival and release times as events you can bill from. A border dwell charge with no timestamps behind it usually gets disputed.


## Failure mode four: treating this as a one-off


Section 338 duties have no sunset. CUSMA now faces a review every year. Canada runs a remission framework for surtax relief, and Statistics Canada noted that some U.S. tariffs announced in August were removed in September. The covered-goods lists will keep moving.


The better answer is to treat the policy calendar as operating data. Effective dates, covered product lists flagged against the customer's commodity master, and the lanes those customers ship on should live in one place. Then, when a date approaches, sales knows which accounts will frontload and dispatch knows which direction will tighten.


## Asset, broker, hybrid: who carries which risk


-


**Asset carriers** carry the directional imbalance on their own trucks and own the source records customs evidence depends on. Their biggest wins come from event-level timestamp integrity and directional pricing.


-


**Brokers** carry quote-validity risk and depend on carrier data they don't capture themselves. Their leverage is in tender terms: required fields at pickup, cargo control numbers on acceptance, and border dwell terms that mirror the customer contract.


-


**Hybrids** can rebalance by moving the soft direction to brokered capacity and keeping assets on the tight side. That only works if their systems price and track each direction separately.


## Where workflow design earns its keep


No two cross-border books look alike. Commodity mix, port pairs, pre-arrival processing habits, and which customs brokers your customers use all shape where things break. That is why generic setups struggle in a month like September, and why the serious operators tune their systems to their own freight.


In practice, that looks like:


-


Status changes that require location and time from the source, with locked or audited edits after the fact.


-


Cargo control and ACI trip numbers as required fields on Canada-bound shipments before dispatch, not optional notes.


-


Commodity flags that mark tariff-exposed customers and lanes, so a coming effective date surfaces the right loads.


-


Directional rate tables with expiry dates the system enforces.


-


Border dwell accessorials calculated from arrival and release events instead of driver recollection.


-


A one-click document packet per shipment (BOL, cargo control document, timestamps) for when an importer or broker asks for proof.


None of this is exotic. It is simply your own rules encoded once instead of rebuilt by hand every time a proclamation drops.


## What to do in the next 30 days


1.


Pull every Canada-bound load picked up between September 4 and September 8 and check whether pickup time, cargo control number, and trip record agree. Fix the process that created any mismatch.


2.


Cut the validity on cross-border spot quotes and add a policy reopener to contract renewals going out this quarter.


3.


Split your Canada–U.S. lane pricing by direction and review margin on each side separately for August and September.


4.


Write a border dwell clause into your rate con template, including when the clock starts and what counts as an importer-side hold.


5.


Build a shared policy calendar that ties effective dates to customer commodities and lanes, and review it in weekly ops.


## FAQ


### Does Canada's September 8 surtax apply to goods that were already moving?


No. CBSA's Customs Notice 26-23 exempts U.S. goods that were in transit to Canada and under a carrier's control when the surtax took effect, as long as the importer has proof such as a bill of lading, report of entry documents, or cargo control documents.


### Does CUSMA qualification protect Canadian goods from the U.S. Section 338 duties?


No. The July 2026 proclamations apply the additional 50% duty to covered Canadian goods whether or not they qualify under CUSMA. Energy, potash, products already under Section 232 tariffs, and certain other goods are excluded.


### Why do Canada–U.S. truck rates keep swinging by direction?


Because shippers move freight ahead of each tariff effective date. That pushed demand southbound before August 22 and northbound before September 8. With capacity near multi-year lows, each pull-forward tightens one direction while the other softens.


### Who pays when a truck waits at the border for customs release?


That depends on your rate confirmation, and many don't address it. Define when the border clock starts, the free time, and who is liable for importer-side holds, then record arrival and release times so the charge holds up.


### Do carriers need a CARM account?


Generally no, unless the carrier is the importer of record. Carriers still need their own CBSA carrier code and must transmit ACI eManifest cargo and conveyance data. Importers and their delegated customs brokers handle accounting and surtax in CARM.
